summary: This informational memo analyzes the Host Density metric used to guide registry allocations of IPv6 unicast address blocks. It contrasts address efficiency in IPv4 allocation with that of IPv6, noting that for large allocations the target efficiency differs very significantly between the two approaches.

eli5.summary: Handing out street addresses to cities by how many houses they have works differently when there are nearly endless addresses. This looks at how fairly and wisely that counting works for IPv6.

questions: what is the host density ratio
subtitle: An analysis of how efficiently IPv6 addresses should be allocated to networks.

tldr.problem: Regional registries allocate IPv6 address blocks using the Host Density Ratio (HD-Ratio) to ensure networks do not run out of addresses too quickly. The current 0.8 HD-Ratio target may be too conservative for large networks, leading to wasteful overallocation.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC analyzes the HD-Ratio metric, compares it to IPv4 allocation practices, and shows that the 0.8 value assumes unrealistically deep hierarchical structures in large networks. It proposes that a higher HD-Ratio (around 0.94) would better reflect how actual IP networks are built.
tldr.outcome: The analysis suggests regional registries should consider revising the HD-Ratio to use address space more efficiently without forcing networks to renumber their customers.

facts.label: Ratio of address consumption
facts.value: 0.8 HD-Ratio uses 7 times more space than 0.94

today: RFC 4692 is an Informational document that analyzes the metrics used by regional registries for IPv6 allocation policy. While it made the case for reconsidering the 0.8 HD-Ratio, the allocation policies of the major regional registries have not changed significantly based on this analysis.

sections.title: The Address Efficiency Problem
sections.content:
When Regional Internet Registries allocate IPv6 address blocks to networks, they use an address efficiency metric to decide how much to allocate. The metric balances two goals: networks should not run out of addresses and need painful renumbering, but the global address space should not be wasted on underutilized networks.

The problem is that public networks, private networks, and different types of infrastructure all have very different structures. The RFC compares how IPv4 allocations work with the framework used for IPv6, and finds significant differences in what efficiency target makes sense.
sections.eli5: When you give out address blocks, you need rules about how full they should be before you hand out more. Too strict and networks run out; too loose and you waste addresses.

sections.title: IPv6 Addresses and the Host Density Ratio
sections.content:
IPv6 global unicast addresses have a 64-bit structure: a 48-bit global routing prefix (allocated to the customer), a 16-bit subnet ID (used within the customer's network), and a 64-bit interface ID (for individual devices). Current policy assumes each customer gets a minimum /48 address block, which provides 2^16 possible subnets.

The Host Density Ratio (HD-Ratio), defined in RFC 3194, measures how many addresses have been allocated relative to how many could theoretically be allocated:

  • HD-Ratio = log(allocated objects) / log(maximum allocatable objects)
  • Values range from 0 to 1
  • The target threshold is 0.8 (80%)

In contrast, IPv4 uses a simple percentage metric: allocate no more than 80% of the available addresses in a block. For IPv4, this works reasonably well. But for IPv6 and large blocks, the HD-Ratio produces very different results.
sections.eli5: IPv6 uses a fancy math formula to measure efficiency instead of just a percentage. The target is an HD-Ratio of 0.8, but the math gives very different answers than simple percentage would.

sections.title: The Problem with 0.8 HD-Ratio for Large Networks
sections.content:
The RFC analyzes what the 0.8 HD-Ratio actually implies by looking at a concrete example. For a network serving 8 million customers, each receiving a /48 address block, the allocation requirements are:

  • With 100% efficiency: a /25 allocation
  • With 80% simple efficiency (IPv4 style): a /24 allocation
  • With 0.8 HD-Ratio: a /19 allocation (64 times larger)

The huge difference comes from what the 0.8 HD-Ratio assumes about network structure. It implicitly assumes that as networks grow, they add many more levels of internal hierarchy. But real IP networks typically use only 2 to 4 levels of hierarchy, not the 10+ levels that the HD-Ratio formula implies for large blocks.

A more realistic model, assuming 75% efficiency at each level with up to 6 levels of hierarchy, yields an HD-Ratio of about 0.94. This allocates much more efficiently than 0.8 while still being conservative about growth.
sections.eli5: The 0.8 HD-Ratio assumes networks get more and more complicated as they grow. Real networks do not. So it wastes a lot of address space compared to a more realistic model.

sections.title: Real-World Impact on Address Consumption
sections.content:
The RFC simulates an IPv6 registry using actual IPv4 allocation data from 1999 to 2004, applying various HD-Ratio values. The results show dramatic differences:

  • HD-Ratio of 0.80: consumes address space equivalent to /14.45
  • HD-Ratio of 0.94: consumes address space equivalent to /17.26
  • Ratio between them: 7 times more address space consumed by the 0.8 target

The impact is not spread evenly. Most allocations (74% to 95%) are small /32 minimum blocks, unaffected by the HD-Ratio choice. But for the remaining larger allocations (especially the largest 2%), the choice of HD-Ratio has enormous impact. These large allocations drive overall consumption due to a heavy-tail distribution.
sections.eli5: Using the 0.8 HD-Ratio burns through IPv6 addresses 7 times faster than using 0.94 for the really big networks, which are the ones that matter most.

sections.title: Rethinking the HD-Ratio Value
sections.content:
The RFC argues that the 0.8 HD-Ratio model does not fit how IP networks are actually deployed. Real networks do not add levels of hierarchy as they scale up the way the 0.8 formula assumes. The alternatives are also problematic: the fixed 80% efficiency model used in IPv4 puts too much burden on network operators to achieve very high utilization at every level, leading to renumbering or NAT deployment to meet targets.

The RFC concludes that a higher HD-Ratio value, such as 0.94, would more accurately reflect the structure and routing characteristics of deployed IP networks, while still being conservative about preventing address exhaustion. This would allow more efficient use of the IPv6 address space without forcing networks into painful renumbering when they grow.
sections.eli5: The RFC suggests raising the target to 0.94, which matches how real networks actually work and wastes less address space without pushing networks to renumber.
